I’d have to measure the dropout on the regulator to see what the true power supply range would be and maybe come up with a way of having a selectable 3.3V/5V IO voltage (though the former would be relatively weak coming from the internal regulator).

The power transistors for this would actually be quite small since the current consumption of standard cell logic, even for a dense 1x1 chip, should be pretty low. I think the full regulator could fit in a corner of the core area without taking up too much space. I’d have to use my run 2 chips to collect more data on my SCL.
If the 3.3V is also to supply the IO, it can be beefed up to 1A relatively easily while still not taking up too much space. For reference: my charge controller has a third of a 1x0p5 core area filled with just PFETs and that can conduct 110A according to SPICE. So, yeah, don’t need much FET to get 1A.

I think this would be cool - it's a small step from here to a SoC that can run straight off USB (you'd just need a 48MHz clock from somewhere to do data).  If you're doing that this offer might be of interest: https://discord.com/channels/1361349522684510449/1361349523724570941/1550939705410064526

It's important for a couple reasons:

1 - startup native vt device creates a current that shuts itself off once the bandgap starts up, causes the right side VBE to go up first. That creates a voltage delta in the amplifier

2 - the amplifier needs current otherwise it doesn't do anything, tail resistor with negative VTH means I don't need some kind of NMOS turnaround mirror. And the current is pretty stable because it's roughly always 0.5-0.6V

3 - amplifier input common mode voltage is quite low and to keep things simple I want NMOS input with PMOS mirror with PMOS CS output to reduce systematic mismatch from different Vds on input pair

4 - native VT devices typically match a lot better than full VT devices, important when it directly impacts bandgap voltage
also just fyi there's no degrees Kelvin....
at high temps the VBE goes down and the VTH goes down as well, the leakage will get pretty bad eventually
note that the threshold voltage by process is fairly wide and kinda symmetric around 0V for nvt-nmos on gf180mcuD
that should be fine, you get a decent amount of sub threshold current at -0.1vgst
could you use the output voltage to trip some turn-off/gate in the startup current path?
unlike celsius and fahrenheit, there's no degrees for Kelvin, just like there's no degree volts.

so basically you have two approaches:
1: buffer the bandgap voltage and compare a scaled version of it to the VBE of a diode temp sensor
2: make a PTAT current loop at the center of the power FET and compare that with the CTAT VBE of a diode sensor at the same location

the only cheap way to get real good voltage control though I've seen so far in LDOs is to have a factory trimmer DAC inside and use the set resistor just to feed an ADC that then tells the trimmed DAC which of a dozen or so of tabulated charge end voltages to aim for.

1 is usually easier to do because you typically have that already on the chip, but it's less accurate
2 is more accurate but it has its own complications
as long as the large-ish resistors don't need to be in the middle of the power FET structure some bipolar's for PTAT/CTAT shouldn't be a problem, I _think_
but like, I dunno that well
one complication with approach 2 is that you can't really guarantee you have 0 temperature gradient, and that can cause your PTAT to do all sorts of weird things

also we don't need to truly measure we just need to start throttling down over a wide enough temperature range to not cause any too high frequency thermally-coupled oscillations in charging power, and throttle to close enough to zero current before the power fet gets so hot that the chip burns out in like less than 5 years of being "plugged in", usually
it's of particular concern if you have a fault condition that causes sudden power draw where you definitely will have a temperature gradient
oh yeah the only think I can reasonably promise is that the center is gonna have approximately average temperature, and under reasonable conditions not too much delta to the hottest
IMO tbh bonus points if the measurement solution somehow allows having a few smol sensors spread about in a grid pattern and perform some osrt of soft-max by way of how it works
Hmmm if you want to really do like granular temp sensing you basically just need an ADC
I think the diode approach would do that but not so sure about how strong the soft-max effect would turn out to be
Just shove a IZTC into a diode and measure the voltage using an ADC
oh no not granular as such, just soft enough action to not form a relaxation oscillation through a temperature reservior
